name: Skin-care baseline routine

lead: The baseline routine is a gentle cleanser, a moisturiser and a daily broad-spectrum sunscreen. People use it to get clearer, smoother, more even skin and to slow visible aging, and communities treat it as the foundation before adding any active ingredients or procedures.

The chain: cleansing removes oil and residue, moisturiser slows water loss from the skin, and sunscreen filters UV light that drives sunburn, photoaging and skin cancer. Sunscreen has the most research behind it, with studies reporting reduced sunburn and skin cancer risk and slower photoaging. Dermatology sources describe the same trio as the generally favoured approach, with other products reserved for conditions like acne.

paras: Cleanse in the morning and evening, moisturise after, and apply sunscreen each morning, reapplying when outdoors for long. Most people start here and add other products only once the basics are steady. Skin changes from sun protection build over months and years.

Risks are low. Fragrances or preservatives can cause contact dermatitis, harsh cleansers or over-exfoliation can irritate, and sunscreen protection depends on how much is applied. Paraffin-based moisturisers carry a documented fire risk near flames.

chain: Healthier skin barrier, less sun damage
angle.text: Cleanser, moisturiser and daily sunscreen are the base layer people build skin quality on, aiming for clearer, more even skin and slower visible aging. Sunscreen works by blocking the UV that drives photoaging, and studies back that part most strongly.

lead: The skin-care baseline routine is the minimal regimen of gentle cleansing, moisturising and daily sun protection that many appearance-focused communities treat as the foundation of better-looking skin before any active ingredients, procedures or other interventions are added. Followers use it to keep skin clean, comfortable, even-looking and protected from the sun damage that drives visible ageing, which they see as groundwork for every other skin goal [1][2].

Wikipedia's skin-care article says dermatologists generally prioritise a foundational routine of gentle cleansing, moisturisation and sun protection, with other products reserved for specific conditions such as acne [1]. Sun protection has the most research behind it. A 2013 randomised trial of 903 Australian adults reported that daily broad-spectrum sunscreen use over 4.5 years was associated with 24 percent less skin ageing than discretionary use, and no detectable increase in ageing in the daily-use group [3]. Wikipedia describes photoaging as changes induced by chronic UVA and UVB exposure, such as wrinkles and pigmentary changes, and lists sun protection as the most effective primary prevention [4].

For cleansers and moisturisers in healthy skin, Wikipedia notes that little is known scientifically about the clinical benefit of simple habits such as washing and applying lotion, and that routines often reflect personal preference; it also says anti-ageing claims on cosmetic products are generally unproven [1]. No trial has tested the three steps together as a package for perceived attractiveness.

paras: The routine has three components. A cleanser removes dirt, oil and product residue; a moisturiser adds or retains water in the outer skin layer; and a broad-spectrum sunscreen filters ultraviolet radiation [1]. In looksmaxxing communities it is often presented as the first tier of skin improvement, ahead of retinoids, acids, microneedling or clinic procedures, with targeted actives added once the basics are in place.

Synthetic detergent cleansers, or syndets, are mildly acidic to neutral (about pH 5.5 to 7) and are generally recommended for people with skin conditions, whereas traditional soaps are strongly alkaline (about pH 8.5 to 11) and can disrupt the skin, although they remain widely used [1]. Wikipedia notes that terms such as mild or gentle are not clearly defined on labels, and that overwashing can dry skin [1].

Moisturisers slow transepidermal water loss using occlusives, which form a barrier layer, and humectants, which attract water [1][5]. Petrolatum is described as among the most effective occlusives, though some people dislike its greasy feel [5]. For eczema, moisturisers improve comfort and may reduce flares, but no single format (lotion, cream, gel or ointment) has been shown clearly superior [5]. Wikipedia reports that a moisturiser with niacinamide and glycerin applied twice daily helps strengthen skin and reduce dryness [1].

Sun protection factor (SPF) measures protection against burning UVB radiation but not UVA, which is why broad-spectrum products are generally recommended; most people apply less than the amount used in testing, lowering the protection actually obtained [2]. Dermatology guidance summarised in encyclopedic sources advises SPF 30 or higher with regular reapplication, including after sweating or swimming [1][2]. Sun-protective clothing and limiting midday exposure are also listed as prevention [4].

Sunscreen may help prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, while evidence for basal cell carcinoma is more limited [2]. The Nambour trial, published in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2013, randomised adults under 55 to daily or discretionary sunscreen, with or without beta-carotene; the daily group showed a 24 percent lower skin-ageing score (relative odds 0.76), beta-carotene had no overall effect, and the authors noted some missing outcome data and modest power [3]. A smaller study reported improvement in photoageing signs with daily SPF 30 over 12 weeks [2].

For cleansers and moisturisers in healthy skin, Wikipedia describes the evidence base as thin and describes terms such as cosmeceutical as marketing terms with no scientific evidence behind them [1]. Excessive exfoliation and hot water are noted as possible irritants, and fragrance and some preservatives can cause contact dermatitis in moisturisers [1][5]. For established photoageing, Wikipedia describes topical tretinoin as the most effective treatment with randomised-trial support, which is the usual next step in communities after the baseline routine [4].

Within appearance-improvement communities the baseline routine is commonly described by proponents as low-cost, low-risk groundwork for skin quality, which they say contributes to overall facial attractiveness. Adherents typically describe adding targeted actives only after the three basics are in place.
No studies found that evaluate the three-step routine as a single combined regimen. Studies of individual components exist, most notably the 2013 randomised sunscreen trial described above [3].

timeline.event: Nambour randomised trial reports less skin ageing with daily sunscreen use over 4.5 years.[3]
